post.title: Training Skills, Not Weights: A Close Read of SkillOpt
post.description: A study log of Microsoft Research's SkillOpt: training reusable Markdown skills for frozen LLM agents with epochs, learning rates, and validation gates.
post.excerpt: SkillOpt treats a Markdown skill document as the trainable parameters of a frozen LLM agent. I forked the Microsoft Research repo to understand what a deep-learning training loop looks like when the gradients are text edits. Here is how it works, how to run it, and where its limits are.
post.content:
Full disclosure before anything else: SkillOpt is not my project. It is a Microsoft Research codebase (the paper is Yang et al., arXiv 2605.23904, with fifteen authors), and my fork at `aryateja2106/skillopt` has exactly zero commits of my own. It is already 163 commits behind upstream, which is itself a small story about how fast this research area moves. This post is a study log: what the system does, how you would run it, and why I think the core idea matters to anyone building agents.

The README's pitch, lightly paraphrased: train agent skills like you train neural networks, with epochs, mini-batch sizes, learning rates, and validation gates, but without touching model weights.

## The problem: two bad options

If your LLM agent underperforms on a task, you have two options today.

Fine-tune the weights. Expensive, and often impossible when the model sits behind an API.

Or hand-tweak the prompt. That is what most of us actually do, and it is ad-hoc: no validation, no history, and every "improvement" risks a silent regression somewhere else.

SkillOpt makes the second path systematic. It treats a Markdown "skill document", the instructions you would normally paste into an agent's prompt, as the trainable parameters of a frozen model. Then it optimizes that document with the full machinery of a deep-learning training loop: batches, epochs, a learning rate, LR schedulers, validation gates, checkpointing, and resume.

The output is a plain-text artifact, `best_skill.md`, that you can read, diff, and drop into any agent's prompt. The trained "weights" are a file a human can review. That property alone got my attention.

## How it works

The core is a six-stage loop, documented in `docs/guide/training-loop.md`:

1. **Rollout.** A "target" model executes a batch of tasks with the current skill document in its prompt. Each task yields a trajectory plus a score from a task evaluator. That evaluator is the loss function.
2. **Reflect.** A separate "optimizer" model analyzes the trajectories, especially the failures, and emits structured edit patches: the text-space analog of gradients. Reflection has a shallow mode (per trajectory) and a deep mode (cross-referencing multiple failures to catch systemic issues). The engine lives in `skillopt/gradient/reflect.py`, and its docstring calls it the "ReflACT core Reflect engine", a trace of the project's lineage.
3. **Aggregate.** Semantically similar patches are merged.
4. **Select.** Edits are ranked and clipped. The `learning_rate` parameter is literally the maximum number of edits applied per step, with cosine, linear, or constant schedulers to decay it over training.
5. **Update.** The selected patches are applied to the skill Markdown.
6. **Gate.** The updated skill is evaluated on a selection split, a held-out validation set, and the update is only accepted if performance improves. Validation-gated SGD for text. This is the trust mechanism: prompt engineering with regression tests built in.

Two extra mechanisms run at epoch boundaries. **Slow Update** (from epoch 2) rolls out the previous epoch's skill and the current one on the same samples, classifies every item as improved, regressed, persistent_fail, or stable_success, and writes high-level guidance back into the skill document. It is a text-space answer to catastrophic forgetting. **Meta Skill** accumulates cross-epoch strategy notes, a compact memory of what the optimizer learned about optimizing, and feeds them back as context in future reflection steps.

## Running it

Python 3.10+, MIT license. Install from source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/microsoft/SkillOpt.git
cd SkillOpt
pip install -e .
```

(Small confession: the README in my fork still points at the upstream URL, which tells you exactly how much I have changed.)

The ALFWorld embodied-agent benchmark needs extras:

```bash
pip install -e ".[alfworld]"
alfworld-download
```

Credentials come from an env file:

```bash
cp .env.example .env
source .env
```

One gotcha the README calls out: `AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT` is always required, or "all LLM calls will fail". Other backends use `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or `QWEN_CHAT_BASE_URL`.

Training a skill on SearchQA:

```bash
python scripts/train.py \
  --config configs/searchqa/default.yaml \
  --split_dir /path/to/searchqa_split \
  --azure_openai_endpoint https://... \
  --optimizer_model gpt-5.5 \
  --target_model gpt-5.5
```

The model names are Azure deployment-name placeholders from the README, not availability guarantees. Any YAML config key is overridable from the CLI: `--num_epochs`, `--batch_size`, `--workers`, `--out_root`. Configs inherit from `configs/_base_/default.yaml`.

Data is your job. You provide train/val/test split directories of JSON task items; no benchmark datasets ship with the repo. Six adapters live under `skillopt/envs/` (SearchQA, ALFWorld, DocVQA, LiveMathematicianBench, SpreadsheetBench, OfficeQA), plus an `_template` for wiring up your own environment.

Every run writes a structured output directory: `config.json`, per-step history, a skill snapshot per step (`skills/skill_vXXXX.md`), a `runtime_state.json` checkpoint, and the final `best_skill.md`. Re-running the same command auto-resumes from the last completed step.

Evaluating a trained skill without training:

```bash
python scripts/eval_only.py \
  --config configs/searchqa/default.yaml \
  --skill outputs/my_run/best_skill.md \
  --split valid_unseen \
  --split_dir /path/to/split \
  --azure_openai_endpoint https://...
```

`valid_unseen` is the test split; `valid_seen`, `train`, and `all` also work. There is an optional Gradio dashboard too:

```bash
pip install -e ".[webui]"
python -m skillopt_webui.app
```

It serves on port 7860 (add `--share` for a public link). After install, two console entry points map to the same train and eval scripts:

```bash
skillopt-train   # scripts.train:main
skillopt-eval    # scripts.eval_only:main
```

## The analogy is literal, not decorative

What makes SkillOpt more than a metaphor is that every deep-learning concept maps to a concrete mechanism (`docs/guide/dl-analogy.md` has the full table):

- Learning rate: the max number of edits applied per step
- Gradient clipping: edit ranking and selection
- Momentum: the Slow Update epoch mechanism
- Early stopping: gate patience
- Transfer learning: seeding a run from an existing skill document

The upstream authors' own guidance, their findings and not mine: cosine schedules beat constant ones, a moderate learning rate of 4-16 edits works well, and 2-4 epochs is usually enough. Skills converge much faster than neural nets, and bigger rollout "batch sizes" hit diminishing returns because the cost unit is API calls, not FLOPs.

Two design choices I keep coming back to as an agentic engineer. First, optimizer and target are decoupled backends (Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, or local Qwen via vLLM on either side), so the model that reflects on failures and writes edits does not have to be the model executing tasks. Second, the repo ships execution harnesses that drive the Codex CLI and Claude Code binaries as the frozen target (`codex_exec_path` and `claude_code_exec_path` in the base config, backends in `skillopt/model/`). You can train a skill file for a coding agent whose weights you will never touch.

## Honest limitations

- **This is not my work.** My fork has 0 commits ahead of `microsoft/SkillOpt` and sits 163 behind; the last commit is by upstream author Cuzyoung. All credit goes to the Microsoft Research team.
- **I have not executed these commands.** They are transcribed from the README and cross-checked against files that exist in the repo (`scripts/train.py`, `scripts/eval_only.py`, the `pyproject.toml` entry points). I had no dataset available to run a real training job, so treat this as a close reading, not a field report.
- **No datasets included.** The README is explicit: prepare your own data.
- **Alpha software.** Version 0.1.0, self-classified as `Development Status :: 3 - Alpha`.
- **API-heavy and Azure-first.** Training burns API calls by design, the docs themselves note diminishing returns from larger rollout batches because of cost, and the hard `AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT` requirement is awkward if you are not on Azure.
- **No numbers here, on purpose.** No benchmark scores appear in the repo files I read. The results live in the arXiv paper, which I have not gone through yet, so I will not quote them secondhand.

## What's next

Three things, in order:

1. Prepare a small train/val/test split and run the SearchQA config end to end, so the commands above become verified instead of transcribed.
2. Point the Claude Code harness at my own agent workflows and see what a trained `best_skill.md` looks like for real tasks.
3. Diff the `skills/skill_vXXXX.md` snapshots across a run. Watching a skill document learn, edit by gated edit, is the most interesting debugging surface I have seen in a while.

My fork is at [github.com/aryateja2106/skillopt](https://github.com/aryateja2106/skillopt), but start with the real thing: [github.com/microsoft/SkillOpt](https://github.com/microsoft/SkillOpt).
